tags.gist: Frames the central challenge as keeping consequential behavior attributable, reconstructable and governed as models, tools and workflows change, not only competent at one point.
Supports the risk-proportionate competency direction with qualifications: risk modifiers, system-assurance mechanisms, root-cause-capable monitoring and an execution-authority distinction for agents.
States that being technically capable does not establish clinical supportability, permission to rely on an output, or authority to execute an action.
Asks FDA to assess a reconstructable event record for higher-consequence devices linking patient, evidence, versions, configuration, tool use, output, reliance and outcome.
Lists ten recommendations, from risk modifiers and configured-device evaluation to event-level evidence, hybrid reassessment, evaluable supervisors and agentic authority characterization.
Calls the two axes a useful, intuitive and scalable primary heuristic and urges FDA to keep them rather than build an unmanageable multidimensional matrix.
Agrees that diagnostic, measurement and signal-processing functions deserve special risk consideration because users cannot directly check their outputs.
Wants traceability, reversibility, time pressure, downstream safeguards, user capability and execution authority as modifiers that shift placement and required controls.
Wants assurance proportionate to how much of the clinically relevant system state sits beyond the sponsor's control, such as external models, tools and data.
Wants directiveness assessed functionally by what a reasonable user would do, weighing specificity, imperative strength, confidence display, urgency and suppressed alternatives.
Would not treat patient-facing status as automatically higher risk, relying instead on calibrated uncertainty, scope limits, escalation and designs that curb automation bias.
Treats the generalist-specialist split as a context modifier and wants required domain knowledge and specialist review built into the workflow, not just labeling.
Wants transition testing of whether a device notices a conversation crossing into patient-specific direction, adjusts safeguards and keeps enough history to reconstruct it.
Wants both escalation errors measured as distinct classes against prespecified, context-justified thresholds rather than one accuracy figure.
Finds the competency approach useful and appropriate, especially its focus on the final configured device rather than the bare model.
Calls competency necessary but not sufficient, since it does not show the right context, current evidence, unchanged configuration or authorized action; adds proportionate assurance functions.
Agrees the axes can scale evidence but wants continuous scaling rather than rigid bins, with least burdensome meaning tailored, not least, control.
Calls the elements a strong foundation and wants benchmark records to preserve test asset, versions, configuration, scoring and adjudication so results stay reproducible.
Wants benchmarks counted as evidence only with established construct validity, using prespecified plans, sequestered sets, contamination disclosure and transparent sponsor benchmarks.
Finds the ladder appropriate, with retrospective evaluation for stable low-risk functions, shadow deployment for workflow effects, and prospective studies for high-consequence autonomy.
Wants synthetic and real performance reported separately before any combined estimate, which must justify transportability and weighting, with generation details recorded.
Finds synthetic data useful for rare events and perturbations but wants independent generation, real holdouts and independent adjudication against correlated blind spots.
Wants the comparator to match the intended clinical role and multidimensional acceptance criteria covering omissions, reasoning, calibration, escalation and consistency.
Supports counterfactual comparators where benefit comes from access or speed, if sponsors justify them and separate device-alone, human-alone and team performance.
Sees third parties adding value in custody, adjudication and tool qualification, while avoiding a small mandatory certification market and keeping sponsors accountable.
Wants the framework architecture-neutral, with extra attention for multimodal systems to cross-modal consistency, provenance per modality and one modality silently dominating.
Accepts more postmarket reliance when uncertainty is measurable and rollback feasible, but not for autonomous, severe or hard-to-detect failures.
Wants the three approaches supplemented by event-level evidence for root cause, with a hybrid periodic and event-triggered cadence.
Details the reconstructable event record, which need not reproduce probabilistic outputs or retain all data, using hashes and version attestations instead.
Wants supervisory agents evaluated independently, with observation, recommendation and intervention authority distinguished and any intervention scope reconstructable.
Would translate shared responsibility into defined technical control duties naming who controls, changes and monitors each material state variable, without disclaiming dependencies.
Proposes a change taxonomy from documentary changes to high-consequence changes of function or authority, with re-benchmarking targeted to affected capabilities.
Would shift PCCPs from prespecifying parameter values to prespecifying bounded change classes and the governance process that qualifies, restricts or rolls them back.
Wants verifiable version identifiers, change manifests, regression suites and pinning, with a defined restricted mode when a provider changes the model unexpectedly.
Finds master files useful if current, lists contents, insists they never replace device validation, and suggests attestations and contractual disclosure if participation lags.
Wants higher-consequence agents to characterize tool permissions, action authority, oversight checkpoints, reversibility, error propagation, injection resilience and change control.
Proposes separating governed reliance from governed execution, with non-binary dispositions such as authorized with constraints or requiring supervision.
Wants interoperability treated as an evidence problem so the assurance system can tell which source supplied which information, when and with what provenance.
Repeats the call for regulatory-science work on an outcome-neutral reconstructable event record for higher-consequence devices.
Wants monitoring to move from isolated output sampling toward continuous assurance able to reveal subgroup or environment degradation hidden by aggregates.
Offers a modular seven-stage assurance model from event state through governed data, context, competency, reliance and execution to continuous assurance, scaled to risk.
Wants FDA to regulate safety properties rather than prescribe an architecture, letting sponsors meet the same assurance question in different ways.
Calls the paper a strong foundation that connects risk-proportionate oversight, competency, confirmation, monitoring, foundation models and agentic oversight.
Concludes that model competency must be distinguished from the assurance conditions around a consequential action, since capability does not confer authority.
